items.learnMore:
Fixed versus variable cost

A fixed cost is the same however much you sell this period. A variable cost is paid again for every extra unit. Total cost adds the two, and every later idea in this unit builds on keeping them apart.

Common mistake

Multiplying the whole bill by the number of units. The fixed fee is paid once per period, not once per cup.

items.learnMore:
Cost per unit

Cost per unit is total cost divided by units, which equals fixed divided by units plus the variable cost per unit. It falls as volume grows because the fixed cost is shared by more units, and it approaches the variable cost per unit without reaching it.

Common mistake

Reading a falling cost per unit as falling total cost. Total cost still rises with volume; only its share per unit falls.

items.reference:
Margin and break-even at the stand
contribution margin = price - variable = $2.00 - $0.50 = $1.50
break-even = fixed / margin = 20 / 1.50 = 13.33, round up to 14
13 cups: -$0.50. 14 cups: +$1.00
margin of zero or less: no break-even exists
Why: each unit pays down the fixed cost by its margin, so you divide the fixed cost by that margin.
items.learnMore:
Contribution margin and break-even

Contribution margin is what a unit leaves after its own variable cost. Break-even is the number of units needed for those margins to add up to the fixed cost, rounded up to a whole unit. If the margin is zero or negative, more volume never helps.

Common mistake

Using the profit on the first unit instead of the margin, or forgetting to round up so that the stand ends the day slightly short.

Straight-line amortization

Divide a lump-sum cost by the number of periods it serves, and charge each period the same share. Month-by-month unit economics then reflect the ongoing cost of running the thing, not the date the invoice was paid.

Common mistake

Spreading over the wrong period, such as the contract length when the asset actually lasts a shorter time.

items.prompt: Implement `contributionMargin(price, variable)`: what one unit leaves after its own variable cost.
items.explanation: The margin is the price minus the variable cost. It can be negative when a unit costs more than it sells for.

items.prompt: Implement `costPerUnit(fixed, variable, units)`: the fixed cost spread over the units, plus the variable cost.
items.explanation: Divide the fixed cost by the units, then add what each unit costs by itself.

items.prompt: Implement `totalCost(fixed, variable, units)`.
items.explanation: The fixed cost is paid once, and the variable cost is paid per unit. With zero units only the fixed cost remains.

items.prompt: Implement `monthlyAmortized(total, months)`: an even monthly share of a one-off cost.
items.explanation: Straight-line amortization divides the total evenly across the periods it serves.

items.prompt: Implement `profit(price, variable, fixed, units)`: revenue minus total cost.
items.explanation: Revenue is price times units. Subtract the total cost, which is the fixed part plus the variable part.

items.prompt: Implement `unitsToCover(fixed, margin)`: how many units of a given margin it takes to cover the fixed cost (no rounding).
items.explanation: Each unit covers its margin, so you need fixed divided by margin units.

items.prompt: Implement `remainingBalance(total, months, elapsed)`: how much of the amortized cost is not yet recognized after `elapsed` months.
items.explanation: Each month recognizes total / months. Subtract what has been recognized so far from the total.

items.prompt: Implement `marginPercent(revenue, cost)`: (revenue - cost) / revenue as a percentage.
items.explanation: The share of revenue left after cost, expressed in percent.

items.prompt: Implement `breakEvenUnits(fixed, price, variable)`: the whole number of units needed to cover the fixed cost. If a unit's margin is zero or negative, return `Infinity`.
items.explanation: Compute the margin first. If it is not positive, no volume ever covers the fixed cost, so return Infinity. Otherwise divide and round up, since a fraction of a unit cannot be sold.
items.reference:
Write the function from the formula
margin = price - variable per unit
margin of zero or less: return Infinity
otherwise: round up (fixed / margin)
20, 2, 0.5 gives 14. 20, 0, 0.5 gives Infinity
Why: naming the formula and its failure case first makes the code almost write itself.
items.learnMore:
Turning the model into a function

Break-even, cost per unit and amortization are one-line formulas, but each has an input where the formula stops making sense: zero or negative margin, zero units, zero months. Decide what the function returns or does there before writing the happy path.

Common mistake

Returning a negative or NaN number for the failure case. It looks like a small answer and slips into later calculations unnoticed.
items.reflection: Think of a calculation you do by hand regularly. Which input would make it give a nonsense answer, and what should it do instead?

items.prompt: Implement `remainingAfter(total, months, elapsed)`: the unrecognized part of a straight-line amortized cost. Once `elapsed` reaches `months` it is 0. Throw if `months` is zero or less.
items.explanation: A schedule over zero months makes no sense, so reject it. Past the end nothing remains, which keeps the balance from going negative. Otherwise subtract the recognized part.

items.prompt: Implement `losingSegments(fixed, segments)`. Each segment is `{ name, users, price, variablePerUser }`. Split `fixed` across segments by user count, and return the names (in input order) of segments whose revenue is below their variable cost plus fixed share.

tests.expr: expect(losingSegments(3200, [{ name: "free", users: 40000, price: 0, variablePerUser: 0.275 }, { name: "paid", users: 8000, price: 12, variablePerUser: 0.66 }])).toEqual(["free"])

expect(losingSegments(100, [{ name: "a", users: 10, price: 1, variablePerUser: 1 }, { name: "b", users: 10, price: 0, variablePerUser: 0 }])).toEqual(["a", "b"])

items.explanation: Compare revenue against cost per segment rather than overall. Each segment pays a fixed share proportional to its users plus its own variable cost; the ones where revenue falls short are the losers.
